title: Soft or spongy brake pedal
h1: Why is my brake pedal soft or spongy?
metaDesc: Brake pedal soft, spongy or sinking? See if it's air in the lines, a leak, old fluid or the master cylinder, how urgent it is, and what to tell your mechanic.
synonyms: brake pedal goes to the floor
brake pedal goes down too far
brake pedal sinking at stop light
intro: A brake pedal should feel firm and stop at the same point every time. If it feels soft, travels further than usual or slowly sinks, the hydraulic system that makes your brakes work has a problem. Some causes are mild, but several mean the car shouldn't be driven, so the first question is about how bad it is.
safety: If the pedal goes to the floor and the car barely slows, steer toward a safe place, downshift if possible and pump the pedal several times to try to regain pressure. If braking still fails, gradually apply a mechanical parking brake, easing it if the wheels skid. For an electronic parking brake, follow your vehicle’s emergency procedure. Once stopped, call for a tow.
If the red BRAKE warning light comes on along with a soft pedal, pull over and stop.
If you see brake fluid leaking near a wheel or under the car, don't drive it.

If smoke continues, you see flames or you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone out, move at least 100 feet away and clear of traffic, and call 911. Stay away from the vehicle.

q_severity.q: How does the pedal feel, and how does the car stop?
q_severity.help: Try it parked with the engine running. A healthy pedal feels firm well before it gets near the floor.

opts.a: It goes to the floor or nearly, or the car barely slows down
The pedal is soft and the red BRAKE warning light is on
It slowly sinks toward the floor when I hold it down at a stop
It feels soft or spongy, but the car still stops normally
It went soft after the brakes got very hot, like on a long downhill or while towing

q_stops.q: When you brake normally, does the car still stop as quickly as it used to?

opts.a: No, it takes longer to stop, or I have to push the pedal much further

q_sink.q: With the engine off, check the brake fluid reservoir. What do you see?
q_sink.help: It's a see-through plastic tank near the back of the engine bay on the driver's side, with MIN and MAX marks. Don't open it, just look at the level from outside.

opts.a: The level is below MIN, or there's wet fluid around a wheel or under the car
The level is fine and there's no sign of a leak
I'm not sure / I can't check

q_when.help: If you can, check the brake fluid reservoir too: a see-through tank near the back of the engine bay with MIN and MAX marks.

opts.a: It started right after brake work (new pads, rotors, calipers or fluid)
The brake fluid is below MIN, or there's wet fluid near a wheel
The brake fluid looks dark brown, or hasn't been changed in years
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: Your brakes may be losing pressure. Don't drive the car
result.now: If the pedal goes to the floor and the car barely slows, steer toward a safe place, downshift if possible and pump the pedal several times to try to regain pressure. If braking still fails, gradually apply a mechanical parking brake, easing it if the wheels skid. For an electronic parking brake, follow your vehicle’s emergency procedure. Once stopped, call for a tow.
if: If the pedal firms up after pumping, keep the vehicle parked. Braking pressure can fail again.
If you see fluid under the car or at a wheel, tell the shop. A burst hose or rusted line is a common cause.
If the red BRAKE light is on, or you smell burning near a wheel, mention it to the shop or tow driver.
result.why: A pedal that goes to the floor usually means the hydraulic system can't build enough pressure, often because fluid is leaking out or a seal in the master cylinder has failed. Most cars split the brakes into two circuits, so you may still have some braking, but not enough to stop safely.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak from a hose, line or caliper
causes.clues: Wet fluid near a wheel or under the car, a low reservoir, or the red brake light.

causes.name: Failed master cylinder
causes.clues: No visible leak, the fluid level is fine, and the pedal sinks under steady pressure.

causes.name: A lot of air in the system
causes.clues: Recent brake work, or the reservoir ran dry.

you: From outside the car, look for wet fluid underneath and on the inside of each wheel.
shop: Pressure check of each brake circuit

result.title: Brake fluid may be leaking or low. Don't drive it yet
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If the level is only near MIN, there are no wet spots and the pedal feels firm, worn brake pads may be what lowered the level. Still have the brakes inspected before driving.
Not seeing a leak doesn't prove the brakes are safe. Fluid can leak inside the master cylinder, or somewhere you can't see from outside.
Don't just top it up and keep using the car. Fluid that leaks once will usually leak again, and the pedal can fail suddenly.
result.why: Brakes work by pushing fluid through lines to each wheel. If fluid is escaping or the level is low, air can get in and the pedal goes soft, and the red brake light often comes on as the level drops. A leak can get worse without warning, so it needs fixing before the car is driven.

causes.name: Leaking brake hose or rusted steel brake line
causes.clues: A wet spot along the line under the car, or an older car from a salted-road area.

causes.name: Leaking caliper or wheel cylinder
causes.clues: Wet, oily fluid on the inside of a tire or wheel.

causes.name: Leaking master cylinder
causes.clues: Fluid at the back of the engine bay, below the reservoir.

causes.name: Worn brake pads
causes.clues: The level dropped slowly over months with no wet spots.
causes.against: Pad wear lowers the level but doesn't make the pedal soft by itself.

you: With the engine off, check the reservoir level.
Look for wet, oily fluid inside each wheel and under the car.

result.title: A worn seal, often in the master cylinder, may be letting fluid slip past
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic check it.
if: If the pedal only sinks a little and then stays firm, it may be less serious, but a technician still needs to rule out a failing master cylinder before the car is driven.
If you find a leak or low fluid, tell the shop.
If the red BRAKE light comes on or the pedal reaches the floor, don't try to move the car. Have it towed.
result.why: When you hold steady pressure and the pedal slowly creeps toward the floor with no outside leak, a common cause is fluid slipping past worn seals inside the master cylinder. A shop will usually test the master cylinder and look for leaks before replacing anything. It tends to get worse and can fail when you need to stop hard.

causes.name: Worn master cylinder seals
causes.clues: No visible leak, and the fluid level stays steady.

causes.name: Slow external leak
causes.clues: The fluid level is slowly dropping, or there are damp spots at a wheel or along a line.

causes.name: Leak inside the ABS unit
causes.clues: The ABS light is on.
causes.against: Much less common than a master cylinder problem.

you: Check the reservoir level and look for damp spots under the car and inside the wheels.

result.title: Your brakes may have overheated (brake fade)
result.now: Pull over as soon as it is safe. Because the pedal went soft after overheating, leave the vehicle parked and arrange a tow or an inspection where it stopped. The fault can return even if the pedal firms up after cooling.
if: If the pedal stays soft, tell the tow operator that the brakes may have lost pressure.
Even if the pedal firms up again, have the cause checked where the vehicle is parked or arrange a tow.

If smoke continues, you see flames or you suspect a fire, pull over safely and switch off the vehicle. Get everyone out, move at least 100 feet away and clear of traffic, and call 911. Stay away from the vehicle.
On long downhills, shift to a lower gear so the engine helps slow the car, instead of riding the brakes.
result.why: Hard, repeated braking makes brakes very hot. Brake fluid absorbs moisture over the years, which lowers its boiling point, and boiling fluid forms bubbles that make the pedal soft. The pedal often comes back once things cool, but that doesn't prove the system is healthy. A shop will usually test the fluid for moisture and check the pads and rotors before deciding what needs replacing.

causes.name: Boiled brake fluid
causes.clues: The pedal went soft after a long downhill or towing, and the fluid is old.

causes.name: Overheated pads
causes.clues: The pedal stays firm but the car slows less, with a burning smell.

causes.name: Dragging brake adding heat
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter than the others.

you: Tell the shop about the hill, load and change in pedal feel you already noticed.
shop: Brake fluid boiling point or moisture test

result.title: Air may have been left in the brake lines during the repair
result.now: Call the shop that did the work before driving further. Tell them the pedal feels soft and ask them to check it, either by coming to you or arranging a tow. Braking may take much more force than usual.
if: If the pedal sinks further, goes near the floor, or you have to pump it to stop, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If you see wet fluid at a wheel that was worked on, or the red BRAKE light comes on, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If a caliper or hose was replaced, ask them to check that every connection is tight and dry.
result.why: Any time the brake system is opened, air can get trapped in the lines. Air squeezes where fluid doesn't, so the pedal feels spongy. Bleeding the brakes properly pushes the air out.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines
causes.clues: The pedal was soft right after the work and firms up when pumped.

causes.name: Loose fitting or bleeder screw
causes.clues: Wet fluid at a wheel that was worked on.

causes.name: Caliper pistons not pumped back out
causes.clues: The pedal went low on the first press after new pads, then firmed up after a few pumps.
causes.against: If it stays firm after a few pumps and never goes soft again, this may have been the cause, but mention it to the shop anyway.

you: Look for wet fluid at the wheels that were worked on.
Note whether pumping the pedal makes it firmer.

result.title: Old brake fluid that has absorbed moisture can make the pedal feel soft
result.now: Keep the vehicle parked and have the brakes inspected. A soft or unexpectedly low pedal needs a brake-system check even when the fluid looks dark. Arrange mobile service or a tow.
if: If the pedal gets softer, starts to sink, or goes near the floor, stop driving and have it towed.
If the fluid level is below MIN, or the red BRAKE light comes on, don't drive it until it's inspected. Old fluid doesn't explain a low level.
If the fluid hasn't been changed in years, have the whole brake system inspected at the same time.
result.why: Brake fluid slowly absorbs water from the air. That lowers its boiling point, so small vapor bubbles can form when the brakes get hot, which feels soft or spongy. Old fluid is a possibility to test, not a confirmed cause, so a shop will usually check for air, leaks and master cylinder wear as well. Most manufacturers list a fluid change interval in the maintenance schedule.

causes.name: Old fluid holding moisture
causes.clues: Dark fluid, or no record of it ever being changed.

causes.name: Small amount of air in the system
causes.clues: The pedal firms up when pumped.

causes.name: Aging rubber brake hoses swelling
causes.clues: An older car, with the pedal softest under hard braking.

you: Look at the fluid color in the reservoir.
Check your service records for the last brake fluid change.

result.title: Possibly air in the system or a brake part starting to wear. Get it checked first
result.now: Get the brakes inspected before driving further. Braking may take much more force than you expect. If you can't get it checked where it is, have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to look at it.
if: If the pedal sinks, goes near the floor, or the red brake light comes on, don't try to move the car. Have it towed.
If the fluid level is below MIN, or you couldn't check it, treat it as a possible leak. Not seeing a leak doesn't prove the brakes are safe.
If the pedal gets firmer after pumping it twice, tell the shop. That can point to air or a rear brake adjustment problem.
result.why: A pedal that feels soft but still stops the car often means something in the hydraulic system is giving a little: air bubbles, swelling hoses, or rear drum brakes that need adjusting. These tend to get worse, sometimes suddenly, and a slow leak or a wearing master cylinder can feel the same at first.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines
causes.clues: The pedal firms up when pumped.

causes.name: Rear drum brakes out of adjustment
causes.clues: An older car or truck with rear drums, and the parking brake needs many clicks.

causes.name: Aging rubber brake hoses
causes.clues: An older car, with the pedal softest under hard braking.

causes.name: Master cylinder starting to wear
causes.clues: The pedal also creeps down slowly at a stop.

you: Check the brake fluid level and color.
Note whether pumping the pedal makes it firmer.

result.title: A soft pedal needs a brake check before it gets worse
result.now: Get the brakes inspected before driving further. Braking may take much more force than you expect. If you can't get it checked where it is, have it towed or ask a mobile mechanic to look at it.
if: If the pedal goes near the floor, sinks at a stop, or the red brake light comes on, don't try to move the car. Have it towed.
If the fluid reservoir is below MIN, don't drive it.
Not seeing a leak doesn't prove the brakes are safe.
result.why: Without knowing how the car is stopping, the safe assumption is that a soft pedal means a problem in the hydraulic system. Many causes can be found in a brake inspection, and catching them early helps prevent a sudden failure.

causes.name: Air or moisture in the brake fluid
causes.clues: The pedal firms up when pumped, or the fluid is old.

causes.name: Small fluid leak
causes.clues: The fluid level is dropping, or there are damp spots at a wheel.

causes.name: Wearing master cylinder
causes.clues: The pedal creeps down at a stop.

you: Look for wet spots inside the wheels and under the car.
